passage:
Monday. In the sprint review Harsha said the delivery date looked unrealistic. The manager leaned over the table: "If you can't commit, maybe someone else can take your seat." The room went still. Harsha's throat tightened, and the rest of the meeting went by in a blur.

Wednesday. It happened again over a different point, with a raised voice and a hint about the appraisal. That night Harsha opened a notes file and wrote the dates, the exact words and who was present, then read it back and saw the pattern in black and white.

Next Tuesday. Harsha asked Gargi, a senior from another team, for coffee and showed her the notes. "This is not a disagreement," Gargi said. "It is bullying, and it is not about your work." Together they mapped how to approach HR, and for the first time in a fortnight Harsha's chest loosened.

qa.q: What did Harsha write in the notes file on Wednesday night?
qa.a: Harsha wrote the dates, the exact words and who was present.

qa.q: How can you tell that Harsha felt shaken during the Monday review?
qa.a: Harsha's throat tightened and the rest of the meeting went by in a blur.

qa.q: Why was it useful for Harsha to show the notes to Gargi?
qa.a: The written record made the pattern clear, and a senior from another team could help plan how to approach HR.

qa.q: How did Gargi see what was happening to Harsha?
qa.a: Gargi called it bullying rather than a disagreement, and said it was not about Harsha's work.

grounding: Across three separate days a worker recognises a manager's humiliating threats as bullying, keeps records and seeks a senior ally and HR.

passage:
Bidisha: are you free? I need to tell someone
Zeenat: call me?
Bidisha: can't, still at office. today in the meeting I said the timeline was unrealistic
Bidisha: Mr. Khanna said "one more word and you can forget your confirmation". in front of everyone
Zeenat: WHAT. that's a threat
Bidisha: he's done it before. last month he said I "don't know my place"
Bidisha: I keep thinking maybe I should just keep quiet
Zeenat: listen. that's bullying. it's not your fault for having an opinion
Bidisha: I feel sick every morning before work
Zeenat: then that's serious. are you writing any of it down?
Bidisha: no
Zeenat: start tonight. dates, exact words, who was there
Zeenat: is there a senior you trust?
Bidisha: Mrs. Rao in legal. she's kind
Zeenat: talk to her this week. and HR. and update your CV, just so you have options
Bidisha: ok. writing it all down now
Zeenat: I'm proud of you. you don't have to stay silent forever

qa.q: What did Mr. Khanna say when Bidisha disagreed?
qa.a: He said, "one more word and you can forget your confirmation".

qa.q: How is Bidisha feeling about going to work?
qa.a: Bidisha feels sick every morning and afraid, even thinking of staying quiet to avoid more threats.

qa.q: What steps does Zeenat suggest, and why are they wise?
qa.a: Keep dated records, talk to a trusted senior and HR, and update the CV, because naming bullying and having options means Bidisha need not stay silent forever.

qa.q: How does Zeenat see Mr. Khanna's behaviour?
qa.a: Zeenat sees it clearly as a threat and bullying, not Bidisha's fault for having an opinion.

grounding: A chat shows a young employee whose manager threatens them for disagreeing, who recognises it as bullying, begins keeping records and plans to seek a senior ally, HR and other options.

passage:
At the cooperative dairy office in Anand, Anjali kept the milk collection records. When she pointed out that Rathod sir's new pricing chart underpaid the small farmers, he slammed the register shut. "You're a clerk. Your job is to type, not think. Do it again and I'll see you're transferred to the chilling plant."

The office went silent. Anjali's hands shook for the rest of the day. At home she barely spoke. Maybe she had overstepped.

The next morning Jahnavi, the senior accountant, found her in the storeroom. "I heard. That was a threat, and it's not the first time he's done it. It's not your fault."

"What do I do?"

"Write down exactly what he said and when. I'll write what I saw. Then we both go to the society's chairman, together."

They did, that Friday, with two pages of notes. The chairman asked for the pricing chart to be reviewed, and for Rathod sir to meet him. Anjali also quietly looked at openings in the district office, just to know her options.

qa.q: What did Rathod sir threaten to do to Anjali?
qa.a: He threatened to have her transferred to the chilling plant.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel after Rathod sir's threat?
qa.a: Anjali felt frightened and shaken, her hands trembling, and wondered if she had overstepped.

qa.q: What steps did Anjali and Jahnavi take, and why were they wise?
qa.a: They recorded what happened, went together to the chairman, and Anjali checked other options, so she was not left alone or silent.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi see Rathod sir's behaviour?
qa.a: Jahnavi sees it as a repeated pattern of threats, and makes sure Anjali knows it is not her fault.

grounding: The passage shows a young woman threatened by her manager when she disagrees, who with a senior ally recognises the bullying, keeps records, goes to a higher authority and looks at options.
